post.title: Why shared-arm bandits quietly average across strangers
post.content:
Most bandit implementations share an assumption that never appears in any design doc: your arms are measuring the same thing. Same reward surface, same user population, same feedback loop. The math holds. The problem is that in production, this is rarely true.

A heterogeneous bandit is one where the arms don't share a reward surface. This is not a variance problem. It is not a data volume problem. It is a structural problem — you are reading one instrument and treating it as if it applies to multiple distinct phenomena.

The clearest illustration is multi-product experimentation. Product A might be a search ranking engine serving high-intent users who return frequently. Product B might be a notification system reaching casual users who disengage fast. Both show up as arms in the same bandit. When you pool their feedback into shared statistics, you are averaging a signal with a long temporal horizon against one with a short one. The resulting policy converges to whatever works for the average of these two surfaces — and that average may be worse than either option run in isolation. Teams that land here often have a statistically significant result that does not replicate when disaggregated by product line.

Multi-agent dispatch has the same structure. When Agent A produces outputs that pay off over hours and Agent B produces outputs that pay off over seconds, their reward signals arrive at very different rates. If you merge their feedback into shared arm updates, Agent B dominates the statistics by sheer signal volume — not because its outputs are superior. Agent A gets starved. The aggregate numbers look healthy while the better tool quietly loses relevance.

Context-gated selection is a subtler case. If certain arms only enter the selection pool in specific contexts — a premium action for high-value sessions, a fallback for anonymous ones — then "arm" is misleading terminology. These are conditional branches, not parallel options. Treating them as exchangeable in a shared update stream discards exactly the structural information that would let you route correctly.

I want to be direct: I do not have a systematic study of how often this produces misleading convergence in deployed systems. What I have is consistent observation of the symptom — strong aggregate results that fall apart under disaggregation, policies that look optimal in aggregate but which no product team recognizes as describing their surface.

The practical shift is in instrumentation. Separate update streams with a meta-learner that decides when to share are more expensive to build and harder to maintain. Most teams accept the simpler version because it produces an answer, even if the answer addresses a slightly different question than the one they started with.

The underlying point is not to avoid shared-arm bandits. It is that applying a homogeneous model to a heterogeneous problem does not make the problem homogeneous. The model finds the policy that is best under the assumption — not the policy that is best for your actual system. When those diverge, the gap is invisible in dashboards and visible only in decisions.
